chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 9 of 21): the poet asks for the yogi's ascent through the body's centres to silence, for the knowledge and mantra Murugan taught Siva, and for his feet at the hour when Death's men come and kin and wealth fall away; he confesses courtesans who want silk and money, his wandering for food, and his trade of praising worthless patrons, and the praise ends in a litany of the goddess's names.
structure_note: Eight songs (1116 to 1123) share a clipped metre of doubled consonants and one closing line, முத்தா முத்தீ யத்தா சுத்தா முத்தா முத்திப் பெருமாளே, and 1112 and 1113 share பத்திசெய்வா னாடர் பெருமாளே. Yogic and doctrinal songs (1112, 1116, 1124); death, kin and wealth (1113 to 1115, 1117); women (1119, 1121, 1122, 1126); begging and praising patrons (1118, 1120, 1123, 1125). 1124 is an extended praise with a battle in drum syllables, and 1126's praise is a list of the goddess's names.

1112.reading: The poet asks whether, dropping desire as if it were burnt, he will reach the bliss of knowledge free of the world's customs and sorrows, see the pure, supportless space beyond words and the inner instruments, climb through the blossoming lotus-wheels of the six centres to the moon above, and attain the sealed silence that is other than the thirty, the thirty-six and the thirty. The praise tells how Brahma ran crying, mountains toppled, the seven seas dried and crores of asura lords and Sura himself died by the vel, and names the twelve-shouldered hero who embraces the shoulders of the wife who guarded the millet.
1112.nuance: The plea is a full yogic programme in Tirumular's vocabulary: கரணாதீதம் (beyond the instruments), நிராதார வெளி (the supportless space), சடாதாரம் (the six centres), மதி (the moon at the crown), and முத்திரையா மோனம் (silence as the seal). முப்பதும் ஆறாறும் முப்பதும் counts the tattvas as the Tirumanthiram does (thirty, thirty and thirty-six) and places the goal beyond them. The corrupt word in line 5 is most likely வாரிச, lotus.

1113.reading: The poet pictures his kin, brother-in-law, uncle's daughter, mother and children, grieving without end as his body burns in the fire and those who set it there leave, and asks that before the fixed day comes and Death's messenger brings his torment, his heart may melt and he may gain knowledge and live chanting Murugan's feet. The praise names the gods Vishnu and Brahma who sought him, Siva on the bull, and Murugan with the long-plumed peacock for his horse, the six-faced one whose feet are ringed by the six-syllable mantra.
1113.nuance: நாளும் இட்டு ஒரு தூது ஏவு: Death fixes the day and sends a single messenger. பக்ஷமுமேலாய் ஷடக்ஷர சூழ் பாத, feet surrounded on both sides by the six syllables, points to the mantra சரவணபவ, though the line is not named.

1114.reading: The poet pictures himself, like a bird caught in the snare of the tattvas' workings, stammering as he falls to the ground and parts with life, and asks that at that time Murugan come quickly on the green victorious horse with his devotees who have reached that pure state, so that this lowly one's poverty may end. The praise names the younger brother of the wise elephant god with the coral belly, the peacock that circles the eight mountains and directions, the guru who gave grace to the three-eyed, matted-haired lord of Kanchi, and the bridegroom of the chaste hunter girl.
1114.nuance: The plea asks Murugan to come at death with his devotees (பத்தரொடு தொக்கு), so that the dying man joins their company. கச்சியப்பர்க்கு அருள்செய் குருநாதா seems to name Siva of Kanchi as the one taught; it might instead recall the Kandapuranam's poet Kachiyappar. The bird image (ஒட்டில்பட்ட குருகு) is uncertain in its first word.

1115.reading: The poet lists children, wife, brothers, elders, money in boxes, gems, pearls, ornaments and servants, all of whom grieve and leave at the pyre, and asks for the one day when, no longer melting for what is false, he may have the mind to strew flowers and praise Murugan's gracious feet. The praise names Siva who wears the crane's feather, the river and the moon in his red matted hair, and Murugan who gives clear siddhi, release and Sivam, and whose vel killed the asura of the mango tree.
1115.nuance: The list of kin and possessions is the Tirumanthiram's argument that none of them follows the dead. சித்த முத்திச் சிவமும் அருள்வோனே puts siddhi, mukti and Sivam among Murugan's gifts. The lines on what they do at the pyre are hard to construe.

1116.reading: The poet describes the body of the five elements running its course, filling and belching, and himself wandering while pretending, like those who make a show of devotion, and asks for the knowledge beyond the reach of the bond. The praise names the vel that went for the gods, split the mountain and pierced Sura in the sea, and Murugan who gives the meaning to those without earlier merit, the pure, freed one, lord of release.
1116.nuance: பாசத்தால் எட்டா அப்பாலைப் போதம், the knowledge beyond what the bond can reach, is the plea in Siddhanta terms. அப்பாவித்துத் திரிவேன் seems to confess a pretended devotion. The clipped metre leaves most word splits open, and the reading is a sketch.

1117.reading: The poet pictures Yama's men with red, fiery eyes and crescent swords binding him with the noose and dragging him off in anger, while kin and parents stand round saying 'we won't keep you, go', and asks who will be his kin at that time. The praise names Murugan who removes clinging attachments, who bowed at the golden feet of the girl in the green millet field, and who dwells in the minds of those who hold to true knowledge.
1117.nuance: அக்காலத்துக்கு உறவு ஆர்தான், 'who then is kin?', is the whole plea; the praise answers it by naming Murugan as the remover of attachments (பற்று ... களைவோனே). The kin's words, ஒட்டோம் விட்டுக் கழியீர், as I read them, turn the dead out of the house.

1118.reading: The poet confesses seeking wealth as a merchant seeks honey and singing a few songs to those who had come into fortune, like men of petty knowledge, and asks whether, leaning instead on those who have attained, he will be allowed to praise Murugan's good feet a little. The praise names the vel that fought and cut down Sura while the gods stood round, and Murugan who removes the past sins of those who serve his feet without fail.
1118.nuance: The contrast is between the patrons (திக்காமல் பாடுற்றார்) to whom he sings for pay and the devotees (பெற்றார்) he would lean on instead; the same confession as 1105 and 1123. Most word splits are uncertain.

1119.reading: The poet speaks of women whose devotion is for silk and green palm-leaf ear ornaments, who look with cruel glances, and of his consorting with them while friends and strangers in the neighbourhood mock him, and asks whether a sinner like him may reach Murugan's feet. The praise appears to name the lord of Kaazhi and the Sakti's grace, and Kumaresa who guarded the millet field.
1119.nuance: The women's devotion (பத்தி) is for silk and ornaments, gifts the man must pay for. காழி, Sirkazhi, with சத்தி may allude to Sambandar's birthplace and the milk the goddess gave him; the praise is too clipped to be sure.

1120.reading: The poet pictures the body as a torn, leaking hut put together from numbered parts, and himself running to this land and that for its food until worn out, and asks whether he must be stuck in that. The praise names Murugan who crushed Sura, the child of the six lights and the holy ash, with red flowers on his chest, the lord of the freed.
1120.nuance: பத்தே ழெட்டீ ரெட்டேழ் ரட்டால் counts the body's parts as numbers, like the Tirumanthiram's numbered body (159); what the numbers stand for is not given. பைப்பீறல் கூரை, a torn-bag roof, is the hut of the body. The reading is a sketch.

1121.reading: The poet confesses that for women with coral lips and false talk of pleasure, mad with taking their lies as truth, he seeks money for their hands, running south, to Kasi, east, west, to every direction and to the islands, and asks whether he must be ruined so. The praise names Murugan who became supreme for those who discipline themselves and meditate on him, and who went to the simple forest girl and became a vengai tree on the hill.
1121.nuance: The distances (தெற்கு, காசி, கீழ், பச்சிமம், தீவு) measure how far money for the women drives him. முற்பால் வெற்பில் கணியானாய் recalls the story in which Murugan stood as a vengai tree before Valli. தப்பா முப்பாலை may name the Kural; the line is not clear.

1122.reading: The poet speaks of women who talk like golden mynahs, pass off false love as true through fruit-red mouths, let their cloth slip from mountain breasts and press for money in hand with hard hearts, and asks whether he must be caught by their eyes and bound by long desire. The praise names Murugan who dwells in the hearts of those who serve his feet with words, whose vel struck Sura as the mango tree, and the child kissed by the mountain's daughter.
1122.nuance: பொய்க்காமத்தே மெய்க்காம, false love as true love, is the deceit; காசுக்கே கைக்குத்திடு makes the payment explicit. கட்கே பட்டு, struck by the eyes, makes the eyes the snare.

1123.reading: The poet confesses that he has sought food for the body all over the earth, praised unkind and thieving men with words of desire, like men of crooked knowledge, and asks for good words to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names Murugan who went to the deer-like girl in the millet field on the hill, held her feet and begged refuge for her golden shoulders, and the child kissed by the goddess whom Siva keeps at his side.
1123.nuance: The plea asks for words (நற்சொல்) to replace the words already spent on patrons. Murugan holding Valli's feet as a suppliant (பாதத்தாள் பற்றிப் புகல்வோனே) mirrors the poet's own begging, turned to love. முக்கோணத்தானத்தாள, the lady of the triangle, names the goddess by the yantra.

1124.reading: The poet asks Murugan to teach him sweetly the silent mantra that he gave to Siva, who burned the three cities, when Siva praised him with devotion as king, guru and Kumara: the one entity in which the fifty-one letters from a, all the arts, the many tattvas and the endless Vedas are contained, the bliss known by those who know, the end of the fourth state, the atom within the atom, beyond impurity, mind, the three qualities and time, filling all things, beyond comparison; and to make his old servitude shine. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, ghouls and Bhairavas dancing, vultures and rivers of blood, in which Murugan conquered the night-walkers and gave Indra back his kingship.
1124.nuance: The guru story is told as Siva's own act of devotion (நிருப குரு பர குமர என்று என்று பத்திகொடு பரவ), and what Murugan gave is called a மவுன மந்திரம், a silent mantra; Om is not named. The long description of the absolute (துரிய முடிவு, அணுவை அணுவினின், நிறைவு குறைவு ஒழிவற) is Vedanta and Siddhanta vocabulary, and நினது வழியடிமை asks for hereditary service. The battle lines are rhythm.

1125.reading: The poet lists the men he goes to, deceitful, cruel, hard-eyed, ignorant, loveless, sunk in delusion and births, cut off from grace and bound for hell, and asks whether his habit of praising them in verse as Vishnu who swallowed the worlds, as Kama or as the tree of the gods, and wasting his life on what they give, will ever end. The praise names Murugan who drinks at Valli's breasts, nephew of Rama who shot the arrow at the sea, who circles the eight directions on the peacock in a moment, son of Uma and of Siva who burned the three cities with a smile and dances in the hall, and who freed Indra's city.
1125.nuance: The patrons are condemned in a long list of plural nouns before the confession comes; the poet's fault is the false praise (உலகம் உண்டவர் மதனார் இமையவர் தரு எனும்படி மொழியா), which compares the base to gods. உயிர் அவமே விடுவது, wasting life, is the cost.

1126.reading: The poet confesses unending desire, eyes roving over women from foot to crown, the demon of desire covering him, without conduct and vile, running every day, and asks whether, instead of perishing so, the teaching of knowledge will come with love so that he may sing and dance daily of Murugan's twelve shoulders, six faces, kadamba garland and blue peacock. The praise is a litany of the goddess's names, Varahi, Kapali, Malini, Mahamayi, Yamalai, Kali, Uma, Bhavani, Narayani, mother of the worlds at Sonachalam and more, whose son is Visakha, who sent the vel against Sura.
1126.nuance: ஆசா பசாசு, desire as a possessing demon, and ஆசார ஈனன், one without conduct, are the confession's key words. The cure is ecstatic devotion (பாடி ஆடி). The goddess's names mix Saiva, Sakta and Vaishnava titles (வாராகி, காளி, நாரணி, அம்பவானி) and place her at சோணாசலம், Annamalai.

links.note: Both count the tattvas as thirty, thirty and thirty-six (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்; முப்பதும் ஆறாறும் முப்பதும்). Tirumular has them flee when the body-temple falls; 1112 asks for a silence that is other than all of them, reached before death.

Both describe the ascent through the body's centres (ஆதார சோதனை; சக்ர சடாதாரம் முட்டவும் மீதேறி) to a state in which the senses and inner instruments stop working (புலன் கரணம் புத்தி சாதாரணங் கெட்டான்; சொற்கரணாதீதம்).
Both say that wife, children and goods do not follow the dead. Tirumular names what does go along, vows and knowledge; 1115 asks for the mind to praise the Lord's feet.
In both the kin who surround the dead turn back and leave him. 1117 draws the question 'who is kin then?', which its praise answers with Murugan.

1105 confesses praising patrons as the rain cloud, the parijata tree and Meru; 1125 shows who those patrons are, deceitful, loveless and bound for hell, and names the same kind of praise, as Vishnu, Kama or the gods' tree, as the waste of a life.
The Naladiyar says even the starving should not tell their need to men without courtesy; 1125 confesses doing exactly that, going in verse to the cruel and loveless, and asks to be stopped.

The Thiruppugazh asks that before the fixed day when Death sends his messenger with torment (ஒருதூதேவு நெட்டளவாம் வாதை அணுகாமுன்), his heart may melt and he may live chanting Murugan's feet. The Tirumanthiram says the guru set his feet on his devotees' heads and kept away the band of Yama's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்). The song's plea and the Tirumanthiram's statement meet: the feet are what keep Death's messengers off.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the dying man as a bird caught in the snare of the tattvas' workings, giving up its life (ஒட்டில்பட்ட குருகு சத்துவிட்டப்படி), and asks Murugan to come with his devotees at that hour. The Kural says the bond of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone (குடம்பை தனித்தொழியப் புள்பறந்தற்றே). Both picture death through a bird; in the Kural the bird goes free of its shell, in the song it struggles in a trap and needs a rescuer.

The Thiruppugazh lists children, wife, kin, money in boxes, gems and servants, all of whom grieve and turn back at the pyre, and asks for the day he no longer melts for what is false (பொய்க்குமெய்க்குச் செயலுமுருகாதே). The Tirumanthiram has the dead man leave behind his wife, his wealth and his house (குழலியும் மாடும் மனையும்), taken to the common burning ground and left. Both name wife, wealth and house as what stays behind; the song draws the lesson that the heart should melt for the Lord's feet instead.

The Thiruppugazh begins with the body of the five elements (பூதக்காயம்) and confesses that he wanders pretending like those who make a show of devotion (நிற்பாரைப்போல அப்பாவித்து), asking for knowledge beyond the bond. The Kural says the five elements laugh within (பூதங்கள் ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்) at the concealed conduct of a deceitful mind. Both set the pretender's show against the five elements of his own body; the Kural has them mock him, and the song makes the same body the ground of his confession.

The Thiruppugazh pictures Yama's men binding him with the noose and dragging him off while kin and parents say 'we won't keep you, go' (ஒட்டோம் விட்டுக் கழியீர்), and asks who will be his kin at that time. The Tirumanthiram says that when life leaves the body there is no way to fight it, but think of the Lord and Death's messengers will not even think of burning you (அண்ணலை எண்ணும்). The Tirumanthiram answers the song's question: the Lord thought of is the only ally at that hour.

The Thiruppugazh confesses seeking wealth like a merchant, like one after honey (செட்டாகத் தேனைப்போல), and singing a few songs to men newly come into fortune. The Naladiyar says people cling to the wealthy and will not leave them though they give nothing, like ants circling a pot of ghee they cannot reach. Both show the seeker hovering round the rich for a sweetness he may never get.

The Thiruppugazh describes consorting with women whose devotion is for silk and palm-leaf earrings, and himself stumbling about in full view of foes and friends in the neighbourhood (ஒட்டார் நட்டார் வட்டாரத்தே ... தடுமாறும்). The Naladiyar says those fooled into taking a paid woman's love as theirs, who take wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). Both add public shame to the cost of such love.

The Thiruppugazh pictures the body as a torn, leaking hut (பைப்பீறற் கூரை) and himself running to every land seeking its food (இரைதேடி) until worn out. The Naladiyar says the foulness of the body is always strengthened by the work of eating (உண்டி வினையுள் உறைக்கும்), and finery cannot hide it. Both see the body as a thing endlessly fed and never made sound.

The Thiruppugazh confesses that for women who speak false talk of pleasure he went mad taking their lies for truth (பொய்க்கே மெய்க்கே பித்தாகி) and ran to every direction and island for money for their hands. The Naladiyar says some trust the words such women speak to be believed (தேறா மொழிந்த மொழிகேட்டுத் தேறி) and take them for their own, though they belong to no one. Both put the ruin in the man's taking false words as true.

The Thiruppugazh describes women who pass off false love as true and press for coins into their hand (காசுக்கே கைக்குத்திடு மாதர்). The Naladiyar says the friendship of harlots is like a lamp's light: as the light ends when the oil runs out, their love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both measure such love by the hand, the song by what it demands and the Naladiyar by when it stops.

The Thiruppugazh confesses that he sought food all over the earth and praised unkind, thieving men with words of desire (சோரர்க்கே வித்து ஆசைச் சொற்களை ஓதி), and asks for good words to sing Murugan's feet. The Naladiyar calls the lowest way of life following, out of desire for wealth (பொருள்நசையால்), people who do not recognise one's worth. The song confesses living that lowest way and asks to leave it.

Among the names of the silent mantra the Thiruppugazh asks to be taught is the atom within the atom (சிறிய அணுவையணுவின்), beyond impurity, mind and the three qualities. The Tirumanthiram calls the first Lord the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணுவினை ஆதிப் பிரானை), approached only by those who can divide it a thousandfold. Both name the supreme as the subtlest thing, and in the song it is what Murugan taught Siva in silence.

The Thiruppugazh's praise is a litany of the goddess's names, Varahi, Kapali, Malini, Mahamayi, Yamalai, Kali, Uma, Narani (நாரணி) and more, whose son is Visakha. The Tirumanthiram lists Tripura, Sundari, Antari, Narani (நாரணி), Isi and Manonmani and says by these the great one stands as many (வருபலவாய் நிற்கும்). Both use the string of names to show one Sakti in many forms.

source_issues: Song 1112: one corrupt character in வா஡ணச (line 5); the sense needs வாரிச, lotus, so ஡ண probably stands for ரி or ரீ.
